transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

I guess what finally made me come in is… I’ve been getting really jumpy, like way more than feels normal for me. I work at a front desk, so there are noises all day, people coming in and out, doors shutting, luggage wheels on the floor, that kind of thing. But lately if a door slams or someone rolls a suitcase fast across the lobby, I jump like something is happening all over again.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I’ll be sitting there trying to look professional, and then this loud sound happens and my whole body reacts before I can even think. My heart starts pounding, and I have to take a minute to get it back down. It’s not like I’m choosing to be dramatic or anything—it just hits me, and then I’m standing there trying to pretend I’m fine while I’m still kind of shaken. That’s really what pushed me to make the appointment.
When you say it feels like 'something is happening all over again,' does that remind you of a specific event or experience you've had in the past?

Yeah… yes. It’s tied to this thing that happened at work with a guest at the counter.

I don’t know why my brain keeps grabbing that exact moment, but it does. I’ll be doing something totally ordinary, like answering the phone or looking up a reservation, and then out of nowhere I get this picture in my head of him leaning over the front desk, like coming into my space, and knocking the equipment toward me. It’s not like I’m sitting there trying to think about it. It just kind of flashes in, very clear, and for a second I’m right back at the counter instead of just taking a normal call.

It’s weird because nothing might even be happening in front of me at that moment. I can be polite on the phone, saying the usual scripted stuff, and inside I’m suddenly seeing that guest over the counter again and the stuff coming at me. Then I have to sort of pull myself back and remind myself, okay, I’m just at work, this is just a phone call, nobody is doing that right now.
Since that incident at work, have you found yourself avoiding certain people, places, or situations that remind you of what happened?

Yeah… I have. More than I wanted to admit at first, honestly.

At work there’s this one part of the lobby, right by where it happened, and I know it probably sounds kind of ridiculous because it’s just a floor and a counter and the same lobby I’ve walked through a thousand times, but passing that exact spot makes my chest tighten up. It’s like my body recognizes it before I even fully think about it. I’ll be walking that way and suddenly I just get this strong feeling of, no, don’t go over there, get away from it.

So I’ve started taking the back hallway whenever I can. Like if I need to get from one side to the other, instead of cutting through the lobby the normal way, I’ll go around the longer way through the back. It’s not always convenient, and I feel a little stupid doing it, but it feels easier than walking past that spot and having my chest clamp down like that. I’m not even sure I decided to do it at first—it just became this thing where I’d automatically choose the route that didn’t make me feel so… trapped or on edge.
Since that incident happened, have you noticed yourself feeling on edge, afraid, or in a bad mood more often than not, even when you're not at work or in the lobby?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t know if I’d say “afraid” all the time, exactly, but I have noticed I’m a lot more short with people than I usually am.

Like, I’m normally pretty careful with coworkers because, you know, at the front desk you kind of have to keep your tone even. Even if things are busy or someone asks you the same question three times, you just answer it. That’s part of the job. But lately I’ll hear myself giving these clipped little answers over nothing, and then afterward I’m like, why did I say it like that?

The other day someone asked me to repeat a confirmation number, just a normal thing, not rude or anything, and I snapped back this really short answer like they were bothering me. It wasn’t yelling, but it had this edge to it. And I could hear it as it came out, which made me feel bad, because they didn’t do anything wrong. It’s like I’m already wound tight, so little things that I would normally just handle feel irritating before I even have time to think.
Have you noticed that these feelings of being short-tempered or irritable stick around even when you’re not thinking about the incident or in the lobby?

Yeah, it does. That’s the part that’s been bothering me, because it’s not only when I’m standing near that spot or actively thinking about what happened.

I’ll be doing something completely normal, like just working through the front desk routine, and someone will ask me a simple question — like to repeat a confirmation number or clarify something I just said — and I’ll answer in this really short, sharp way. Not screaming or anything, but definitely not my usual tone. I can hear myself doing it, too, almost as it’s coming out, and then I feel bad because the person didn’t do anything wrong.

I’m usually pretty careful with coworkers and guests. I try to keep things smooth, keep my voice even, because that’s part of the job. But lately it’s like I have less room inside before I get irritated. Little normal things feel like they hit a nerve faster than they should, even when I’m not consciously thinking about the incident.
Do you find yourself being extra watchful or easily startled even in places that aren’t related to work, like at home or when you’re out running errands?

Yeah… yeah, I do. I mean, it’s not constant every second, but I’m definitely jumpier than I used to be.

The thing that really made me feel like, okay, something is not right here, is how I react to sudden noises now. If a door slams, even if it’s just somebody coming in too hard or the wind catching it or whatever, I jump like my whole body gets yanked. And at work, if someone rolls a suitcase fast across the lobby — that loud rattling sound — I’ll flinch before I even realize what it is. It’s like for a second my body thinks it’s happening again, even if my brain catches up and goes, no, it’s just luggage, it’s just a door.

And then it takes me a minute to settle back down. My heart starts going fast, and I have to kind of stand there and breathe and act normal, because obviously I’m at the desk and people are looking to me to be calm. But inside I’m trying to get my heart back down and not look like I just got scared by nothing. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because these are normal sounds. Doors slam. Suitcases roll through lobbies all day. But lately they hit me really hard.
Since the incident happened, have you found yourself feeling angry, guilty, or ashamed about what occurred or your reaction to it?

I don’t know… not in a clear way, I guess.

I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m walking around thinking, “I’m angry about this,” or “I’m ashamed,” exactly. It’s more muddled than that. Sometimes I do get frustrated with myself, like if I react strongly to something or if I’m not acting like myself, then I’ll think, come on, why are you doing that? But I don’t know if that’s guilt or shame about the incident itself.

And angry… maybe irritated, but I don’t know that it’s anger at what happened. I haven’t really sat there and thought it through like that. It’s more like I’m just thrown off, and then annoyed that I’m thrown off, if that makes sense. But I wouldn’t say guilt is a big thing I’ve noticed. Shame, maybe a little embarrassment about how I’m handling things, but not some constant feeling of shame about the incident.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy since the incident happened?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as hopeless, no. I don’t think I’ve been walking around feeling like there’s no point to anything or anything that strong.

Feeling down… maybe here and there, but it’s hard for me to separate that from just being tired and stressed out by how off I feel lately. Like, I’ll have moments where I’m quieter than usual or I don’t really feel like talking much, but I don’t know that it’s the same as being depressed. It’s more like I feel worn out and kind of preoccupied.

As far as losing interest in things, I haven’t really noticed a big change there. If anything, I still want to do normal things, I just don’t always feel as relaxed when I’m doing them. But I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped caring about things I usually enjoy. It’s not like I’ve lost interest in everything. It’s more that my mind feels… distracted, I guess.
Since the incident, have you found yourself feeling persistently fearful, angry, or emotionally numb specifically related to what happened at work?

I don’t think I’d say persistently, no. I mean, I do feel unsettled when I think about work or when something reminds me of it, but “persistently fearful” sounds like I’m scared all the time, and I don’t think that’s quite right.

Angry… not really. I get frustrated, like I said, mostly with how I’m reacting or how hard it is to just feel normal, but I’m not walking around with this steady anger about what happened.

And emotionally numb… I don’t know. I don’t think so. I still feel things. Sometimes maybe I kind of shut down for a minute or don’t want to talk about it, but I wouldn’t describe myself as numb exactly. It’s more like I’m trying to keep moving and not get too caught up in it. Like I’m aware of it, and it bothers me, but I don’t feel completely cut off from my emotions or anything like that.
Since the incident at work, have you had days where you feel emotionally flat or detached, like you’re going through the motions without really feeling present?

Yeah… I think maybe that has happened, but not all day or anything like that. It’s more like these little moments, especially when I’m back near the front desk.

Like I’ll be standing there in the lobby, doing the normal receptionist stuff, answering a question or looking at the computer, and for a few seconds it feels… I don’t know, kind of distant. Like the lobby is real, obviously, and I know where I am, but it feels sort of unreal or far away, like I’m watching myself do the job instead of fully being inside it, if that makes sense.

It doesn’t last long, and I can usually just blink or focus on what I’m doing and keep going. But it’s strange. I wouldn’t say I feel totally numb or like I’m not myself for hours. It’s more these brief flashes where I’m present enough to function, but I don’t feel completely there.
